lines.text: Alignment: where your data starts in memory, and why it matters.

lines.on_screen: Heading, a row of 12 empty boxes, addresses 0–11 appear
lines.text: Memory is a long row of boxes. Each holds one byte. Its number is its address.

lines.on_screen: Boxes 0–3 fill teal, brace “x[0]”; then x[1], x[2] at 16.7 s
lines.text: A floating-point number, an f32, takes four bytes. Then the next one, and the next.
An array of f32 is just these four-byte groups, side by side, no gaps.

lines.on_screen: Fade; heading “The cache works in 64-byte lines”; strip of 48 small boxes
lines.text: Let’s zoom out. Each small box is now a whole float: four bytes.

lines.on_screen: Three cache-line bands appear with names
lines.text: The cache doesn’t fetch single floats. It moves memory in sixty-four-byte lines: sixteen floats per line.
Here’s the key point. The line edges are fixed by the hardware: zero, sixty-four, one twenty-eight. You can’t move them.

lines.on_screen: Heading changes; one 4-float box highlighted: “one load = 16 bytes”
lines.text: NEON, the phone’s vector unit, reads sixteen bytes at once: four floats in one instruction.
So a loop walks through an array in sixteen-byte steps.

lines.on_screen: “Case 1: the array starts at 0”; array fills blue; arrow at byte 0; eleven loads drop in, counter stays at 0
lines.text: Case one. The array starts at zero, right on a line edge. Watch the loads.

lines.on_screen: All eleven loads in place, all teal
lines.text: Four loads fill each line exactly. Not a single load crosses an edge.

lines.on_screen: “Case 2: the array starts at byte 4”; strip clears, array refills shifted; arrow at byte 4
lines.text: Case two. Same array, same loop, but it starts just four bytes later.
Watch the fourth load.

lines.on_screen: Load 4 turns copper and flashes; both lines pulse
lines.text: There. It crosses the edge.
And there’s another.
Every fourth load sticks out over an edge, so it touches two lines.

lines.on_screen: Braces over the first split load: “12 bytes in line 0”, “4 bytes in line 1”
lines.text: Look closer. Twelve of its bytes come from line zero, and the last four come from line one.
That’s called a split load.
A split load still gives the right answer here. It just costs extra work.
How much extra, on this core? That’s something Phase 1 will measure.

lines.on_screen: Heading; rule “aligned to N = multiple of N”; at 123.6 s the code line address % N == 0
lines.text: Now the word itself. An address is aligned to N when it’s a multiple of N. In code: address modulo N equals zero.

lines.on_screen: Table headers; row 1024: yes yes yes
lines.text: Ten twenty-four is a multiple of sixty-four: right on a line edge.
Ten forty divides by sixteen, not sixty-four. No splits, but not a line edge.
Ten twenty-eight is only a multiple of four. Loads will split.
The rule: start every array at a multiple of sixty-four, and no load ever splits.

lines.on_screen: Heading “What Rust promises today”; card Vec<f32>
lines.text: What does Rust promise today? A Vec of f32 only promises what a float needs: a multiple of four.
In practice it’s often better aligned. But often is luck, not a promise.

lines.on_screen: Second card: aligned buffer, multiple of 64
lines.text: So in Phase 1 we build a small buffer whose start is always a multiple of sixty-four.
Then every benchmark starts from the same layout, every single run.

lines.on_screen: Fade; “In three lines”; point 1 appears at 182.8 s
lines.text: In short: cache lines are sixty-four bytes, fixed edges.
Our code reads sixteen bytes at once.
Start arrays at a multiple of sixty-four: no split loads.
